rule: Record what you saw, calculated, feared, and expected—not only the moves played.
Trace the game backward to the earliest decision that created a lasting disadvantage.
When an opening goes wrong, decide whether you forgot a move, misunderstood its purpose, or failed after leaving theory.
Label missed tactics by mechanism such as loose piece, back rank, removal of defender, or calculation cutoff.

principle: Review Time as a Chess Resource
rule: Mark where you spent time, where you moved too quickly, and which positions actually deserved calculation.
For each critical position, list the moves you considered and the strong moves you never generated.

principle: Use the Engine Only After Self-Analysis
rule: Reconstruct the game unaided before consulting engine evaluations and variations.

principle: Extract One Transferable Lesson per Game
rule: Finish analysis with one concrete question or rule you can use in a future position.
When an error pattern repeats, collect positions that isolate the same decision and solve them as a set.
Review winning games with the same rigor as losses, especially positions where the opponent missed a chance.

principle: Index Games by Structure and Theme
rule: Organize instructive games by pawn structure, plan, and error type instead of only by opening name.
Each month, measure recurring errors, slow-game volume, tactical accuracy, and study transfer.
Choose openings that lead to a manageable family of pawn structures and plans.
Establish one sound response to each major first move before adding alternatives.
Against rare moves, understand the opponent's idea and your principled response before memorizing detail.
Map which sequences transpose, which avoid your preferred setup, and where a choice becomes irreversible.

principle: Attach a Why to Every Opening Card
rule: Store the purpose, tactical justification, and intended structure with every move you memorize.

principle: Study Model Games After the Core Line
rule: Once the opening moves are stable, study complete games that demonstrate the typical plans and endings.

principle: Practice Opening Positions, Not Only Moves
rule: Start training games from key repertoire positions and play them against resistance.
At the end of each line, state the pawn breaks, best and worst pieces, exchanges, and opponent's plan.
Replay the same critical structure from both sides with different plans and time controls.

principle: Balance Tactics, Endgames, and Slow Games
rule: Keep all three in the training week, then weight extra time toward the dominant weakness.
Use a small schedule of study, play, analysis, and retrieval that can survive ordinary weeks.
Prefer positions whose strategic demands stretch you without overwhelming your calculation and memory.
Cycle through diagnosis, one priority skill, deliberate practice, slow games, and reassessment.
